column1: # Parse errors, both directions, against build/bin/rexxc.
# One row per program, tab-separated fields.
# `class` says what KIND of answer the oracle gave, and it is recorded per row
# rather than derived from the number at test time:
#   translation  rexxc refused to TRANSLATE the program. This parser must
#                reject it with the same major, sub and line.
#   install      rexxc rejected it, but for something outside the program
#                text: it could not bind the program to a library or an
#                external routine. This parser accepts it, or rejects it for a
#                later error having recorded the directive the oracle names as
#                one whose EXTERNAL it reached first, because loading a library
#                is not parsing. Every install row is a
#                EXTERNAL "REGISTERED x". Two error classes, 98.903 and
#                90.999, so a `98.9xx` prefix rule would miss half of it --
#                which is exactly why this is a field and not a rule.
#                Evidence for the classification, per row: the message names
#                the library or the routine it could not find, never anything
#                about the program text, so the failure depends on the machine
#                and never on the source. A clean-room parser cannot reproduce
#                BOTH CODES FIRE DURING TRANSLATION, NOT AFTER IT. None of
#                the install rows is a ::REQUIRES, which is the only path
#                through the library directive's install step. The sites are
#                inside the parser: 90.999 comes from the ROUTINE directive's
#                external-library handling and 98.903 from the library lookup,
#                which the parser reaches at parse time, both for a routine
#                rexxc has no install step at all, yet reports both. Measured:
#                `nop` then `::routine r external "LIBRARY x"` gives 98.903 on
#                line 2 with rc 158, and `::routine r external "registered x"`
#                gives 90.999 on line 1, both from rexxc alone.
#   -            rexxc answered rc 0. The program translates.
# `inserts` is what the oracle's secondary line (after `Error N.M:  `) shows of
# the message's inserts: one `k=value` item for each insert position `k` the
# oracle's text for `expect` shows, each item ending in `\|`, the value
# escaped as `program` is, or `-` where there is none. The file holds no
# message text: a test renders the text from interrexx's own table. Where the
# oracle's text places two inserts side by side (49.2) the split is not
# determined by the line, and the first insert is the shortest. It is placed
# before `program` so that `program` stays the last field.
# Re-derived from the oracle, and checked against `expect` and `line`, by
# (run from a fresh empty SCRATCH directory)
#   corpus/errors/derive.sh SCRATCH > NEW && mv NEW corpus/errors/parse-errors.tsv
# `expect` is `ok` for an accepted program and `major.sub` otherwise. `line` is
# the line the oracle's MAIN message names, or `-` for an accepted program.
# `program` is the program's bytes, with `\\`, `\t`, `\n`, `\r` and `\xNN` the
# only escapes. It is last because it is the only field that can contain
# The rows cover the programs parsed by the `ok`/`err` helpers of
# case tables of tests/scanner.rs and src/expr/tests.rs (the latter as the
# program `r = <expr>`), the error programs of tests/program.rs, and the
# latter as the `if <condition>` programs). Each row is what build/bin/rexxc
# Nothing here is our parser's own answer. A row records only what the oracle
# said, so a divergence shows up as a test failure rather than as an expected

/* Keywords are not reserved words. Every instruction keyword is also a legal
   variable name, so a symbol is a keyword only by *position* -- first token of
   a clause that is not an assignment. A scanner that classifies keywords
   lexically cannot produce this program's output. */

/* Each of these is an assignment, because the second token is `=`. */
if = 2
do = 3
say = 4
end = 5
parse = 6
then = 7
call = 8
select = 9
when = 10
otherwise = 11
return = 12
exit = 13
signal = 14
trace = 15
numeric = 16

say if do say end parse then
say call select when otherwise
say return exit signal trace numeric

/* The same spelling as keyword and as variable in one clause. */
if if = 2 then say "if-as-keyword saw if-as-variable =" if
                 else say "wrong branch"

/* DO still loops while `do` holds a value. */
do i = 1 to 2
  say "iteration" i "and do =" do
end

/* SELECT/WHEN/OTHERWISE while all three are variables. */
select
  when when = 10 then say "when-as-keyword saw when =" when
  otherwise say "otherwise"
end

/* A stem whose name is a keyword. */
end. = 0
end.1 = 7
say "end.1 =" end.1

/* Keyword as a compound tail, and as a function-call target spelling. */
stem. = 0
stem.if = 99
say "stem.if =" stem.if

/* PARSE using a variable named parse. */
parse value "a b" with first second
say "parsed" first second "while parse =" parse

/* A label may also spell a keyword. */
call trace_label
exit 0

  say "called a label named trace_label; trace =" trace
